newsitem.title: ITALY: Bossi launches fresh attack on Rome establishment.
newsitem.headline: Bossi launches fresh attack on Rome establishment.

text.p: Firebrand separatist leader Umberto Bossi launched a virulent attack on Italy's political establishment on Saturday, saying northerners had nothing to lose but their chains by creating a breakaway state.
"Nothing can escape the Big Brother of the Italian state," Bossi said in a keynote speech to a Northern League congress in Milan. "We have to decide whether we want to live in Italy or in Padania."
Padania is the name the Northern League movement founded by Bossi has given to a self-styled state in northern Italy.
"Italy is finished. We have to get out of here. Let us leave," said Bossi, speaking in front of a poster depicting a missile called "Free Padania" rising out of a swamp.

But he sounded a note of caution on whether conditions were ripe for an early push towards an independent Padania, apparently because opinion polls show scant support in the north for a separatist agenda.

Calls by Bossi and other League leaders for an independent state brought an immediate rejoinder from Prime Minister Romano Prodi who said the cause of separatism could prosper if Italy failed to join a single European currency.
"The League today is a movement which has one sole objective -- that of breaking Italy in two," he told a conference in Rome.

"Our response will be entry into Europe (European economic and monetary union) and the start of a federalist reform which gets underway a measured and strong decentralisation. If we stay out of Europe, the League cashes in."

Prodi hopes membership of a currency union and sweeping institutional reform can undercut support for the League, which rose to prominence on public disgust with political corruption and a crushing tax burden.
The League won more than 10 percent of the national vote in elections last April on a federalist platform fashioned to appeal to Italians in the affluent north.
Bossi abruptly changed tack after the elections, which gave the League its highest number of votes but failed to give him a pivotal role in politics.
He ditched federalism and espoused a separatist creed, but a declaration of independence for Padania fell flat last September, suggesting he had completely misread the popular mood.
An opinion poll published by the Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera suggested that northern Italians had not warmed to Bossi's new separatist program.
The poll said 79.7 percent of 600 people questioned in northern Italy shared President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro's view that Italy was "single and indivisible."
It said 67.9 percent backed the idea of a federalist state and, disturbingly for Bossi, nearly three quarters thought that he was not the right man to look after the north's interests.
The League is forging ahead with plans to organise a referendum in April which will poll support in northern Italy for an independent Padania.
